Q3752768.summary: The Virgin sits frontally on a throne, crowned and wrapped in a red mantle over a blue robe, holding the Christ Child before her with both hands as he sits upright on her lap. Today the statue is enshrined beneath a silver crown held by two angels within a silver wreath. As a 'Seat of Wisdom', she offers the Child to the pilgrims who climb to this high Pyrenean valley.
facts: Although tradition says Saint Giles carved the image while living as a hermit at Núria around 700–703, the statue now venerated is a Romanesque carving of polychromed walnut usually dated to the 12th century.
According to legend the image was found in 1079, together with Saint Giles's cross, bell and cooking pot; the custom of putting one's head into the pot and ringing the bell survives at the shrine.
The Virgin of Núria received a canonical coronation in 1965 and is principal patron of the diocese of Urgell.

links.label: Viquipèdia (Catalan): Mare de Déu de Núria

Q3752768.notes: Wikidata's '9th century' reflects the legend rather than the object; Catalan Wikipedia gives 12th (or 12th–13th) century. This moves the work out of the 8th–11th-century batch.

cur:catacombs-liebieghaus-sarcophagus.summary: At the left a praying woman appears in a round medallion; beside it Christ, among bearded apostles holding loaves, multiplies the bread, with baskets at the base. The deeply undercut heads and drapery give the relief a vivid immediacy.
facts: The museum dates it to about 330 (inv. 1501).

cur:catacombs2-girona-sant-feliu-strigil.summary: Three carved groups punctuate the strigils. At the centre an orant, probably the deceased, stands between two beardless men, perhaps apostles; at the left two soldiers seize Peter by the arms. At the right Christ, holding a scroll in his left hand, heals a blind man, with a bearded apostle shown at smaller scale.
facts: Catalan Wikipedia notes that Christ, though his face is worn, has short curly hair, matching the 'hero Christ' type of the early 4th century.
It has been suggested that the central orant was originally female and was later reworked as a man with a rudimentary beard.

cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-55-christ.summary: Above the psalmist, who points to his eyes and touches his heel watched by hidden enemies, the bearded Christ-Logos — here without nimbus or mandorla — strides forward with a bannered cross-staff and drives back three attackers: 'then shall mine enemies turn back'. Below the hill lies the pit of Hell with the head of Death. Christ appears as an active defender rather than a distant judge.
facts: The Utrecht Psalter illustrates every psalm and canticle with a lively pen drawing — 166 in all — that translates the words of the text, often literally, into images; in these the Lord of the psalms is regularly shown as the youthful Christ-Logos.
It reached Canterbury by about 1000, where it was copied three times in the Middle Ages: the Harley Psalter, the Eadwine Psalter and the Anglo-Catalan Psalter.
cur:manuscripts2-utrecht-psalm-55-christ.notes: The figure of the Lord is identified as Christ (the Christ-Logos) following the commentary of the Utrecht University Library's annotated edition, which describes the psalter's consistent practice of drawing the God of the psalms as the youthful Christ. The image is a crop of the drawing from the library's IIIF image server.

cur:monumental-thessaloniki-hagia-sophia.summary: Seated against the gold of the apse, the Virgin in a deep red-brown maphorion holds the Christ Child before her; he sits frontally in golden robes and blesses with his right hand. Traces of the great cross of the Iconoclast period can still be made out around the figure, which was inserted in its place.
facts: During Iconoclasm the apse held only a large cross on a gold ground; this was later replaced by the image of the Virgin and Child.

Wikipedia dates the replacement to 787–797, after the restoration of icons, while other sources (including the Commons description of this photograph) assign the Virgin to the 11th or early 12th century.

links.label: Wikimedia Commons: Saint Sophia Church, Thessaloniki - Apse mosaic

cur:monumental-thessaloniki-hagia-sophia.notes: Date disputed between the late 8th and early 12th century; y=1000 is a compromise and may need revision.

Q1106387.summary: At the centre of a field of gold reliefs, gems and enamels is an ivory Crucifixion: Christ hangs heavily on the cross under the titulus, between the lance-bearer and the sponge-bearer, with roundels of sun and moon above and a crouching figure beneath his feet. Diagonal bands of pearls divide the gold into compartments with evangelists, saints and imperial donors. Older than the Gospel book it now protects, the cover places the Cross at the heart of the whole design.
facts: Wikipedia notes that the front cover dates from around the 980s and is attributed to the Trier workshop of Archbishop Egbert, while the ivory plaque is stylistically different and its origin much discussed.
Among the gold reliefs are the young Otto III and his mother and regent Theophanu (d. 991), the Virgin and St Peter, and Saints Willibrord, Boniface, Ludger and Benedict.
The Gospel book itself was made about 1030–1050, some fifty years after the cover, and is now in the Germanisches Nationalmuseum in Nuremberg.
Q1106387.notes: The earlier curated text mentioned the rivers of Paradise; English Wikipedia (read) describes the top and bottom compartments as the four evangelists with their symbols, so that claim was dropped.

Q116244842.summary: This small hexagonal censer of silver, partly gilded, hangs from three chains. Under an arcade of twisted columns on each of its six faces stands a gilded holy figure: Christ holding a Gospel book, the Virgin with hands raised in prayer, Saints Peter (with a cross) and Paul, and two winged angels. As incense rose from it during the liturgy, the vessel surrounded worshippers with an image of the heavenly court gathered around Christ.
facts: The Met dates the censer to ca. 582–602, the span of the reign of Emperor Maurice.
Greek inscriptions run along the upper rim above the arcades.
It is small: 8.9 cm high and 13.2 cm across, weighing about 364 g.
Q116244842.notes: Acc. 1985.123. The Met's object page text was not accessible (bot-blocked), so identifications rest on the Met's subject tags (Christ, Virgin, Peter, Paul) and on the photographs; the two winged figures are clearly angels but are not named here. The reason for the precise date range was not confirmed.
